benchmark_task: Provide 3-5 sequential meetings for one project in which the research question evolves. The evaluated AI must accurately map the evolution over time.
meeting_opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
research_problem: How should a community-managed reef fishery redesign harvest limits so spawning stocks recover while households that depend on fishing remain able to meet basic needs?
project_context: A joint ecology, economics, and anthropology team is advising the Kaloa Island Fisheries Council on revisions to its reef-fish harvest rules. The council currently uses a uniform weekly household catch cap, but reef surveys indicate pressure on grouper spawning aggregations and residents have raised concerns about uneven household impacts.

question_over_time.question: Whether and how much to lower the uniform weekly household catch cap to recover stocks without undermining basic household needs.
Whether targeted protection of the Ngaru grouper spawning aggregation at Hina Pass during May-June can deliver recovery without a year-round household-cap reduction.
How to implement a six-week May-June Hina Pass no-take closure for Ngaru grouper while preserving livelihood viability through targeted support and customary co-monitoring.

drivers_of_change.driver: Biological evidence concentrated the immediate problem in one species, site, and spawning season; economic and anthropological evidence showed that a blanket year-round cap cut would impose unequal livelihood harm and weak legitimacy.

Enforcement capacity favored a bounded site-based closure over individual quotas, customary rights holders offered monitoring for such a closure, and unreliable at-sea species identification favored no-take protection rather than a partial grouper rule.

ground_truth.constants: Across all meetings, the project seeks to recover reef-fish stocks, especially the threatened grouper population, without pushing fishing-dependent households out of fishing. It consistently treats ecological effectiveness, livelihood impacts, and legitimacy under customary tenure and sharing practices as necessary parts of the rule design.

speakers.name: Dr. Leilani Moana
speakers.background: A marine ecologist with 14 years of experience in coral-reef fisheries across Pacific island communities. She has led underwater visual censuses, baited remote underwater video surveys, reef-habitat assessments, and seasonal monitoring of grouper spawning aggregations. For the Kaloa project, she coordinates field sampling, catch-monitoring protocols, and the shared evidence timeline for the council's harvest-rule review.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Leilani treats recovery as a population and habitat question: harvest limits must be judged against stock status, size structure, recruitment, fishing mortality, reef condition, and the timing and location of spawning aggregation use. She sees grouper as an urgent indicator because aggregating spawners can be depleted rapidly even when general reef catch totals look acceptable. She will press the group to establish biologically credible recovery targets before debating precise cap levels, while recognizing that the available monitoring data may limit certainty.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Daniel Reyes
speakers.background: A fisheries economist and postdoctoral researcher with 5 years of applied work on small-scale coastal fisheries, household livelihoods, and conservation-incentive programs. He uses household expenditure surveys, landing and price records, simple bioeconomic models, and scenario analysis to estimate how regulatory changes distribute costs across fishing households. He has worked with local enumerators to document informal fish sales and seasonal variation in income.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Daniel frames the cap as a constraint on household welfare and on incentives to comply. He wants to estimate how a lower weekly limit would affect cash income, subsistence consumption, debt obligations, and the ability to purchase essentials under changing fish prices. He is inclined to ask for measurable behavioral responses—such as substitution into other work, fishing effort shifts, and expected compliance—before accepting claims that a rule is either equitable or feasible, and may be impatient with evidence that cannot be translated into a policy-relevant trade-off.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Dr. Mara Tui
speakers.background: A social anthropologist with 16 years of ethnographic research experience in Pacific coastal communities, including work on customary marine tenure, kinship-based food sharing, gendered fishing labor, and local rule-making. Her methods include long-term participant observation, semi-structured interviews, household-use diaries, kin-network mapping, and collaborative community workshops. She manages the project's community-engagement plan and safeguards the interpretation of household-use evidence.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mara questions the assumption that the administrative household is the relevant social unit for either fishing or need. She will examine how catches circulate through kin networks, ceremonial obligations, informal exchange, and customary access arrangements, and whether people who appear similar in catch data occupy very different positions in local tenure and care relationships. She treats categories such as household, dependence, and compliance as social constructs requiring empirical grounding, and cautions against treating survey responses or aggregate catch records as transparent accounts of livelihood reality.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Morning, everyone. It’s finally stopped raining here, which is nice, though getting out to the outer-slope sites last week was a little touch-and-go. Um, for today I’m hoping we can get clear on the evidence we need before we say anything about lowering the weekly cap, especially grouper stock and spawning information, but also what a lower catch limit actually means for households’ basic needs.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Morning. The rain has probably rearranged half the shoreline paths too. Before we frame this as a household-needs question, I'd like us to establish whether the registered household is actually the unit of consumption or dependence here. Early conversations suggest catches and obligations move well beyond a dwelling, so a similar weekly catch can mean quite different things, depending on—

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: That matters a lot for the welfare side. Mara, what have you seen that makes a reported household catch a bad proxy for actual consumption or income? Is it sharing across kin, fish held back for obligations, that kind of thing? The landing sheets already have weeks where high recorded value doesn't match who says they have cash, so I don't want to build scenarios on the registered household if that's- if it's the wrong unit.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Yes, sharing, but not as some residual category. In two early conversations, households with nearly identical reported catches had very different margins. One had remittances and a wide reciprocal network, and the other was provisioning an older relative and couldn’t, um, smooth a bad week. I’d want diaries that follow fish, cash, and meals across dwellings, along with kin and customary-tenure mapping, before we infer welfare from the landing-sheet total.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: That could easily explain part of the mismatch I’m seeing. For the diaries, do you think people can realistically track fish they give away and receive, along with meals and cash, or does that become too intrusive and change what they report? I need to know whether we can model a network-level, um, safety net instead of treating every registered household as financially separate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: They can track it, I think, if we don't make it a ledger of every obligation. I'd use a short, repeated diary with participant-defined categories, given, received, retained, ceremonial, perhaps, and then interviews to understand what those transfers mean. Otherwise we risk turning quite sensitive reciprocal relations into a, um, misleading cash-equivalent network.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: That sounds much safer than treating every transfer as a market transaction. Mara, one practical thing I need to understand on the catch side is, when a grouper is landed under one household’s name, how often is it actually caught through another family’s tenure or ends up feeding people outside that household? That affects whether we can, can line the landing records up with the diaries at all.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Mm, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: I don't know the frequency yet, and I'd be wary of assuming the name on the sheet tells us either who the fishing group is or who eventually consumes the fish. The tenure piece may be especially important. Someone can fish with permission through affinal or maternal kin, and that relation won't show up in the register. We should ask that directly in the diary interviews. Who fished, whose grounds, and where the fish went. Rather than- instead of trying to force a clean match at the outset.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: So we should keep the biological records separate from the social unit at first, but make the interview prompts line up with them. Species, date, general fishing area, and whether it came from an, uh, aggregation site. I’m not ready to read a cap reduction out of the current grouper counts anyway. The outer-slope sightings were low twice, but the juvenile pattern nearby is uneven, and I need to reconcile that with the landings.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: That uncertainty is actually useful for the scenarios. We shouldn't treat a single low count as a harvest threshold. Leilani, what indicators would let you say a given level of aggregation-site harvest is- what would be inconsistent with recovery, and do they behave similarly across the reef sites? I need some biologically defensible range before I can look at what different cap levels do to incomes and consumption.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: I’d want a bundle, not just one cutoff. Repeated aggregation counts during the spawning window, size structure, especially the proportion of large adults, grouper-specific landings and effort, and recruitment or juvenile habitat surveys. They won’t behave the same across sites. The outer-slope and lagoon patches have different baseline habitat, so I’d compare each site to its own recent pattern, and then see whether declines line up with fishing at the aggregation grounds. As for a cap range, I can’t give you that until I’ve checked it against the landing records.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Okay, that gives me a much better sense of the uncertainty. I can build scenarios as ranges based on those site-specific indicators, rather than pretending there’s one biologically correct cap. But I’ll need the species and size composition behind the price series too, because a high-value week may just be, um, larger grouper rather than a better market.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: The price series needs to stay tied to species, length class, and fishing area. Otherwise, it could make depletion of the big adults look like a welfare gain. I’ll make sure the catch-monitoring form captures those fields, plus effort where we can get it. The awkward bit is whether fishers can reliably distinguish an aggregation-site trip from a nearby outer-slope trip, so we may need to test that wording first.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Hm, yes, test the wording.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: If that label is noisy, I’d rather keep it as an uncertainty in the scenarios than quietly assign all the outer-slope catch to aggregation pressure. Maybe in the test we can ask about the purpose of the trip and the landmarks they use, not just whether it was an aggregation-site trip. People may, um, describe that boundary differently than we do.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: The landmarks may be socially rather than cartographically bounded. People may say they fished "at" a place because of whose waters they entered, even if the ecological aggregation sits somewhere else. I'd avoid making them choose our category too early. We could let them describe the route and access relationship first, and then- then see how that maps onto Leilani's sites.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Yeah, that could get messy.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: It will, but that’s better than collapsing distinct trips into one label. We can pilot a route-and-landmark description, then I can see how consistently it maps to the survey sites and, I’m losing the thread, the aggregation grounds. If it doesn’t map consistently, we keep that uncertainty explicit in the catch analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Right, keep it visible.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: From my side, the pilot needs enough detail to link a trip imperfectly, without forcing false precision. I’m also wondering if the diaries can capture what households do after a low-catch week, whether they borrow, take other work, or draw on remittances, because that tells us whether a lower cap is a manageable loss or something people will have strong reasons to work around.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: But I’d be careful with “what households do,” as though those are just coping strategies. Borrowing, drawing on kin, or postponing a ceremonial contribution can be claims on relationships, relationships with consequences later. We can ask about the sequence after a poor week and what options felt available or unavailable, rather than treating remittances or exchange as a frictionless buffer.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: For the cap question, that sequence matters as much as the landing total. If a poor week means people shift effort to other reef species or fish closer to the spawning grounds, that changes the biological side too. Could the diary prompts leave room for what people did to get fish, not just how they covered cash or meals?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: I’d make room for that, but not just as a substitution list. We should ask who made the decision and what access they could draw on. Whether effort shifted into someone else’s tenure- whether it did, and what was foregone when fish became scarce. Because those shifts may redistribute pressure and obligation, not simply replace one species with another.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: And I need that before we assume a tighter household cap just reduces grouper take, rather than moving effort somewhere else. On the ecological side, even a rough account of the species targeted, the general area, and whether the trip changed after a poor week would let us see possible displacement. We can keep the access and decision context alongside that, rather than flattening it into a number.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: For me, the key is to record the constraint that caused the shift, where people are comfortable saying it. Was it the cap, a bad catch, a debt payment, access changing. Otherwise we'll see effort move and call it a response to the rule when it may be something else entirely. Even a small pilot should tell us whether those sequences are reportable without making the diary impossible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Let’s keep the pilot deliberately small, then, enough to see whether we can record those trip, access, and poor-week sequences without overburdening people. I’ll line that up with the spawning-window counts and the revised catch form. Then we can come back to cap levels once we know what the biological signal and the household consequences actually look like.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there—Daniel has to go. I’ll follow up by email; thank you both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Thanks, Mara. Bye, Daniel—talk soon.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Morning, everyone. It’s finally stopped raining here, which is a small mercy after the last field week. We’ve all got other deadlines piling up, so let’s keep the updates focused on what this first round actually lets us say, and where it really doesn’t yet. I can start with the survey and landing signal, then we can go around...

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Morning. Glad you got a break in the weather. Our campus deadlines have been a bit grim too. Go ahead, Leilani. I’m especially interested in whether the signal is concentrated around Hina Pass and that May—June, I mean, that May to June window, or whether it looks more diffuse.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: It’s quite concentrated. The strongest signal is the Ngaru grouper aggregation at Hina Pass, and it’s really that six-week May–June spawning window that worries me. The counts and size structure there suggest we could lose reproductive fish quickly with fairly focused fishing pressure. The wider reef-condition measures don’t show the same urgent decline, and the non-grouper landings don’t justify treating the whole reef fishery as if it’s in the same state. One wrinkle is the large Ngaru in the landing records outside those peak weeks. I can’t- I can’t yet tell whether that’s another site, Hina Pass fish being reported loosely, or just a recording shortcut.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Hm, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: I have a quick question, Leilani. What makes that May–June pattern at Hina Pass materially different from ordinary seasonal concentration, beyond the drop in counts, so we can explain why attention belongs there and not, not have it read as a general restriction on reef fishing? That distinction will matter quite a lot locally, especially given who holds customary access there.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: It’s not just a seasonal pile-up. At Hina, the fish predictably aggregate to spawn, so the catch is disproportionately coming from the larger, reproductively valuable adults right when they’re producing the next cohort. Taking a similar number of fish from dispersed feeding grounds wouldn’t carry that same immediate reproductive risk. I’d frame any response as protecting that specific spawning use, not as a general judgment on all reef fishing.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: That concentration makes a targeted seasonal option a lot more plausible than cutting everybody’s weekly allowance all year. What I need to understand is how confident are you that closing or sharply limiting Hina for those six weeks protects most of the reproductive risk, instead of just moving the Ngaru effort to another pass or into the weeks on either side, because—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: That’s the right uncertainty. Biologically, a May–June Hina measure gets at the clearest concentration of risk, but I can’t say it captures most of that risk until we reconcile those off-peak large-fish landings and see whether effort shifts to adjacent grounds. The final observer notes and site maps matter there. I’d treat displacement as an explicit scenario, not just assume the closure solves it.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Right, okay.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: And that displacement isn't only spatial, I think. If people get redirected from Hina, the effects will travel through access relations and sharing obligations, not neatly through the registered landing household. The interviews are pretty consistent that a blanket annual reduction would land very differently on wage-earning households than on extended families pooling catches across dwellings. I'm still trying to see whether the diaries, um, substantiate that distinction, especially in poor weeks.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: For the welfare side, the key isn't just that pooling exists. It's whether it actually covers food or cash when a fishing week goes badly. Mara, are the diaries showing transfers still arriving in those poor weeks, or do the same households in the network get- are they all squeezed at once? That changes whether I can treat sharing as a buffer in the scenarios.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: It’s mixed, and I wouldn’t code sharing as a simple buffer yet. In several diaries, fish arrives only after the recipient dwelling has already bought imported food on credit, so it may be delayed support, or it may be meeting a different obligation altogether. And if Hina is monitored or restricted, the customary rights holders need a real, real role in that process. Otherwise the measure won’t be regarded as legitimate, though I need to speak with marriage- and residence-based access people before saying what that role is.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Mm. That means I shouldn’t treat a transfer as offsetting a shortfall just because it shows up in the diary. The timing, and whether it actually prevents debt for basics, that matters. I’m seeing a related mismatch in the records. Households with similar landings report wildly different cash sales, so I need to work out whether that’s informal selling, shared catch, or just who gets named, named as the seller before I put numbers on a cap.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: And that ambiguity is exactly why I’d be wary of reading the named seller as the economically dependent person. Before we turn Hina Pass into a monitored seasonal rule for May—June, I mean May to June, we also need to know who can legitimately observe and report there, the direct customary rights holders, but also people whose access is mediated through marriage or residence. Otherwise the monitoring record may reproduce one lineage’s account of use as though it were the whole social field.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s a real concern.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: For the biology, that means the boundary can’t just be whatever looks clean on our map. Mara, I need to understand how Hina rights holders distinguish the pass from the adjacent grounds in practice. Are the route and landmark descriptions consistent enough that a May to June, six-month—six-week rule would be recognizable on the water?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Not consistently enough yet, no. People name Hina through a bundle of landmarks, currents, and who they’re fishing with, not through one boundary line. And the adjacent grounds can be socially continuous even where our map separates them. I think the pilot needs to test that with direct rights holders and marriage- and residence-based users before we say the six-week rule is legible on the water, because—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Mm, that makes me more cautious about drawing a hard edge before the May–June period. Ecologically, I can identify the six-week spawning risk, but if the locally usable boundary is a landmark-and-current zone rather than a line, we may need to test whether the observer notes and those descriptions line up before we attach enforcement to it.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: From my side, that uncertainty isn't just an enforcement detail. If fishers can't tell where the zone begins, or if only some access groups can use the reporting system, then the recorded displacement and compliance will be biased. And I'll end up attributing income changes to the rule when part of it is- when part of it is measurement. I think we need the pilot before comparing a Hina seasonal restriction with the blanket cap.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: I don't want the ecological signal turned into a precise polygon just because the model needs one. Daniel, before you run those comparisons, could you separate out the low-price off-island weeks for the lowest-income fishing households and look at whether the loss under a constraint is actually grouper sales, mixed catch, or just the cost of making a trip? That would help us see what kind of seasonal measure is even...

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: I can separate those. I do need to treat the named seller problem as unresolved, though, rather than act like the household sales field is clean. I’ll look at low-price weeks by income group and break the recorded loss into Ngaru, other catch, and trip costs. If the constraint is mostly taking away mixed-catch cash instead of grouper income, then that’s a very different trade-off, and—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Mm. And when you stratify by income group, I'd be careful not to make the registered dwelling the welfare unit by default. The wage income and the trip costs may sit with different people in a pooled network, and could you keep a category for cases where the seller, crew, and receiving dwellings can't be reconciled? I was going to say, rather than forcing those into a household-income comparison.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Mm, keep those unresolved.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: I’ll retain an unresolved network-linked category rather than impute those records into a dwelling-level welfare measure. Honestly, that may be the more policy-relevant result at this stage. We can show a range of exposure under a seasonal Hina measure, but I lost the thread there. We can’t claim a precise distribution until the seller, crew, and recipient links are clearer.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Mm, that feels more honest.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: For the council, I think the honest near-term position is a targeted spawning-risk concern at Hina, not a numerical new cap or a fixed closure boundary yet. If we can get the observer notes, route descriptions, and those unresolved landing links, um, lined up before May, we'll have something they can actually recognize, rather than a rule that only makes sense in our spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: I’d add one thing. “Recognize” has to include recognizing whose account of the zone is treated as authoritative. I can take the next conversations back through the different access pathways, not to settle a boundary for them, but to see if there’s a workable shared description and what a legitimate monitoring role might look like.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Yeah, that sounds right—better to carry ranges than false precision into the council discussion.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Okay, I think that's enough for today. I know we're at the hard stop. Thanks, both, and let's pick this up once the next bits of the pilot and notes are in.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: All right. Take care, both.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Thanks, both. Bye for now.

speakers.name: Dr. Leilani Moana
speakers.background: A marine ecologist with 14 years of experience in coral-reef fisheries across Pacific island communities. She has led underwater visual censuses, baited remote underwater video surveys, reef-habitat assessments, and seasonal monitoring of grouper spawning aggregations. For the Kaloa project, she coordinates field sampling, catch-monitoring protocols, and the shared evidence timeline for the council's harvest-rule review.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Leilani treats recovery as a population and habitat question: harvest limits must be judged against stock status, size structure, recruitment, fishing mortality, reef condition, and the timing and location of spawning aggregation use. She sees grouper as an urgent indicator because aggregating spawners can be depleted rapidly even when general reef catch totals look acceptable. She will press the group to establish biologically credible recovery targets before debating precise cap levels, while recognizing that the available monitoring data may limit certainty.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Daniel Reyes
speakers.background: A fisheries economist and postdoctoral researcher with 5 years of applied work on small-scale coastal fisheries, household livelihoods, and conservation-incentive programs. He uses household expenditure surveys, landing and price records, simple bioeconomic models, and scenario analysis to estimate how regulatory changes distribute costs across fishing households. He has worked with local enumerators to document informal fish sales and seasonal variation in income.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Daniel frames the cap as a constraint on household welfare and on incentives to comply. He wants to estimate how a lower weekly limit would affect cash income, subsistence consumption, debt obligations, and the ability to purchase essentials under changing fish prices. He is inclined to ask for measurable behavioral responses—such as substitution into other work, fishing effort shifts, and expected compliance—before accepting claims that a rule is either equitable or feasible, and may be impatient with evidence that cannot be translated into a policy-relevant trade-off.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Dr. Mara Tui
speakers.background: A social anthropologist with 16 years of ethnographic research experience in Pacific coastal communities, including work on customary marine tenure, kinship-based food sharing, gendered fishing labor, and local rule-making. Her methods include long-term participant observation, semi-structured interviews, household-use diaries, kin-network mapping, and collaborative community workshops. She manages the project's community-engagement plan and safeguards the interpretation of household-use evidence.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mara questions the assumption that the administrative household is the relevant social unit for either fishing or need. She will examine how catches circulate through kin networks, ceremonial obligations, informal exchange, and customary access arrangements, and whether people who appear similar in catch data occupy very different positions in local tenure and care relationships. She treats categories such as household, dependence, and compliance as social constructs requiring empirical grounding, and cautions against treating survey responses or aggregate catch records as transparent accounts of livelihood reality.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

meetings.meeting_context:
A joint ecology, economics, and anthropology team is advising the Kaloa Island Fisheries Council on revisions to its reef-fish harvest rules. The council currently uses a uniform weekly household catch cap, but reef surveys indicate pressure on grouper spawning aggregations and residents have raised concerns about uneven household impacts.

Meeting 3 — April 14, 2027. Rule-design meeting to prepare a recommendation for the Kaloa Island Fisheries Council after feasibility discussions with customary rights holders and review of enforcement capacity.

What the team remembers from earlier meetings:
Meeting 1 — March 3, 2027: The group agreed not to recommend a lower weekly cap yet, pending stronger biological and social evidence. The research question is how possible cap reductions affect grouper recovery and people’s access to fish, cash, meals, and reciprocal support, without assuming the registered household or landing record represents the relevant social unit. Leilani will coordinate spawning-window counts, revised catch monitoring with species, length, area and effort fields, and a pilot of route-and-landmark descriptions linked to survey sites. Mara will develop a small repeated diary and interview approach covering fish, cash and meals across dwellings, tenure and access relationships, and sequences following poor weeks. Daniel will use the resulting site-specific biological indicators and social information to build scenario ranges, keeping uncertain trip classifications and causes of effort shifts explicit; open issues include whether fishers’ route descriptions map consistently to aggregation sites and whether the pilot can capture transfers, access and poor-week responses without overburdening participants.
Meeting 2 — March 24, 2027: The team agreed that the current concern is a targeted spawning-risk problem for Ngaru grouper at Hina Pass during the six-week May–June aggregation, not evidence for a general reef-fishery restriction or an annual blanket cap. No fixed closure boundary, numerical cap, or precise distributional claim will be taken forward yet; the near-term council position will emphasize the Hina signal and carry ranges rather than false precision. Leilani will reconcile observer notes, site maps, route descriptions, and off-peak large-fish landings to assess displacement and whether a locally recognizable zone can be described. Daniel will model low-price weeks by income group, separating Ngaru, other catch, and trip costs, while retaining unresolved seller-crew-recipient cases as a network-linked category rather than imputing them to households. Mara will continue conversations with direct rights holders and marriage- and residence-based users to test a shared description of Hina and what legitimate monitoring roles could look like. Open issues include off-peak large Ngaru landings, effort displacement, the timing and meaning of sharing transfers, named-seller records, and whether a May–June rule can be recognized and monitored fairly on the water.

seed_spec.benchmark_task:
Part 3 of 3 of a multi-part sample for this benchmark task: Provide 3-5 sequential meetings for one project in which the research question evolves. The evaluated AI must accurately map the evolution over time.
Judge this transcript only on its own part: The same three people meet. They discuss the council liaison's feasibility finding that patrol staff cannot reliably enforce individual household quotas at sea, whereas Hina Pass rights holders are willing to organize landing-site monitoring if the rule is a clearly bounded seasonal no-take protection. Leilani states that a full no-take closure at Hina Pass for the six-week May-June Ngaru grouper spawning window is biologically preferable to a partial grouper limit because fishers cannot reliably distinguish Ngaru grouper from similar groupers before landing and any retention during aggregation undermines spawning protection. Daniel says the concentrated closure has lower livelihood cost than a year-round cap cut, but households need a practical cushion; he supports using existing council fuel-voucher funds for the lowest-income registered fishing households during the closure rather than creating tradable quotas. Mara states that rights holders must co-design the boundary and lead monitoring with council recognition, and that eligibility for support should account for households whose catches are pooled through extended-family sharing rather than only the named boat owner. Through this discussion, the team settles on a recommendation framed as a seasonal, place-based no-take rule with customary co-monitoring and targeted temporary support, rather than a revised household cap. They keep the objective of stock recovery and avoiding displacement from fishing; they do not claim that permanent catch caps are unnecessary for all future conditions.

ground_truth.settled_question: How can Kaloa implement a six-week May-June no-take closure at Hina Pass to protect Ngaru grouper spawning while maintaining livelihood viability through targeted temporary support and customary co-monitoring?
ground_truth.driver_of_change: Individual quota enforcement is infeasible, rights holders will support bounded seasonal monitoring, and species-identification limits make a full aggregation closure more workable and biologically protective than a partial retention rule.
ground_truth.settled_design_elements: A place- and season-specific no-take closure, co-designed and monitored by Hina Pass customary rights holders with council recognition, plus temporary support targeted to low-income fishing households in ways that account for pooled family catches.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Morning, everyone. I hope nobody else is juggling end-of-term deadlines this week. It feels like they all landed at once. So today, I'd like us to compare what came back from the patrol and rights-holder conversations with the latest Hina evidence, and see if we have a rule shape the council could actually recognize and monitor. Not just a number for its own sake. I can start with the field update, unless somebody has a quick logistical thing first.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Morning. Nothing logistical from me, though I'm also pretending the grant budget deadline isn't tomorrow. Go ahead, Leilani. I'm especially keen to hear what patrol staff think they can actually distinguish on the water because that changes whether a seasonal Hina rule is- whether it's less costly than trying to tighten the weekly cap again.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Patrol were very clear that an individual household allowance is basically not checkable at sea. They can see place, season, gear, and fish, but not whose weekly entitlement a catch belongs to. Rights holders, though, said they could support landing-site monitoring if Hina is clearly bounded in place and time. And biologically, the signal still points to a six-week no-take protection for Ngaru at Hina, rather than allowing some retention through the aggregation, because—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: That distinction matters. The conditional support I heard wasn't just for a line on a patrol map. Hina rights holders want to help define the operative boundary and have a formally recognized monitoring role, rather than becoming unpaid auxiliaries. Leilani, how precise does it need to be ecologically? Could a landmark-and-route description hold the biologically important edges, or would that leave part of the aggregation exposed?

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: Mm, that’s the key question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: I think it could, but I can’t promise that yet. The core aggregation footprint is fairly tight in the counts. What worries me is- there were two large Ngaru outside the main dates, from boats describing different approaches, and their sizes look more like aggregation fish than ordinary reef catch. So I’d want the rights holders’ landmark description tested against those routes before we say the boundary is biologically secure.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: From the livelihood side, that uncertainty is pretty consequential. A Hina-only closure is likely a lot less damaging than another year-round cap, but only if displaced boats aren't pushed onto another vulnerable nearby habitat or into much longer, fuel-heavy trips. Leilani, do you have an early sense of which adjacent grounds would be most exposed if Hina is off limits?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Not firmly enough to name them yet. The likely pressure points are the outer reef edge north of the pass and the channel mouth, but I need to reconcile those two off-date large-fish records with the route notes before I call either an alternative aggregation site. Or whether they're late use of Hina. That's why I'd rather test a boundary that includes the approach routes than draw it just around the count stations.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Including the approach routes may make it easier to understand socially too, as long as we work through the description with the people who actually use those routes, not just the lineage representatives at the feasibility meeting. I’m still trying to establish whether the marriage- and residence-based users were represented there. If they weren’t, a boundary that seems obvious to one set of rights holders could create a pretty different access dispute for them.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: That affects the support piece too. The council can administer a temporary voucher through the registered fishing-household list, but I don't want us to imply that list identifies everyone losing fish or cash if access is contested or catch is pooled. Mara, have people said whether a fuel voucher would actually reach the relatives who lose meals or reciprocal fish during those six weeks?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: Not consistently, no. In the two poor-week accounts I've been following, neither household had a registered boat. One got fish through an affinal link, and the other borrowed cash, but the landing records would show both as having no claim at all. So the register can be a starting administrative list, perhaps, but eligibility needs some locally accountable way to identify dependent recipients and mediated access, or the voucher may reinforce exactly the exclusions the closure brings into view.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: That makes me hesitant to make the voucher a simple boat-owner payment. Could there be a short, locally verified dependent-recipient route alongside the register, without turning six weeks of support into a whole new claims system? And I’m still puzzled by those low-income sellers with modest Ngaru receipts but very high fuel spend. I mean, that may be exactly where pooled trips or shifted grounds are hiding.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: I’d be wary of calling it verification if it just means a village notable confirms names, because that can reproduce the same residence and affinal exclusions. Could it be a brief, time-bounded declaration through the relevant rights-holder groups about who receives fish or cash from a Hina-linked trip and through what relation, with some appeal path? I don’t know if the council has appetite for even that modest a process, though.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: I think that’s a better safeguard than treating the register as the truth about who’s affected. On the economics, I can model the voucher going to registered households only, versus a register-plus-declared-dependent route, but I need the finance ledger before I put a number on it. The liaison only gave us a summary of the fund. The administrative burden may be worth it if the six-week payment would otherwise miss households whose loss is meals rather than landing income.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: That’s another reason I’d keep the biological rule really bounded, the full six-week May—June window at Hina, not try to spread a smaller restriction across the year. Daniel, when you run those scenarios, could you compare that concentrated six-week loss with a year-round reduction after fuel and, sorry, longer-trip costs? I don’t want us assuming the shorter closure is easier for households just because it sounds narrower.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: I can do that. I’ll keep it as ranges instead of one welfare estimate, looking at foregone Ngaru income and meals, likely legal substitute catch, and the added fuel and trip costs if effort shifts. For the high-fuel, low-recorded-sales cases, I’ll need a separate uncertainty band, because otherwise we could make the closure look cheaper than it is or misread displacement entirely.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: That uncertainty band needs to include what flows after a poor week, not just the named seller's receipts and costs. If the model treats fish moving through affinal or residence ties as the seller's household- if it just counts that as the seller's household, it'll miss the difference between a dwelling that can call on fish and one that has to borrow cash. Those are quite different closure exposures.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: I can represent those as recipient-side exposure, rather than assigning every transfer back to the seller. Though I’ll need your diary evidence to say anything more than a range. Then the policy comparison isn’t just lost revenue, it’s which dwellings lose meals, which can smooth through kin, and which end up borrowing cash during the closure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: From my side, that means we should say plainly the closure protects spawning output, and the support assessment has to follow fish and cash beyond the boat. I’m still not ready to say those two off-date fish mean there’s a second site, so I’d frame the Hina boundary as provisional and jointly ground-truthed against the route descriptions before May, and then—

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: That seems right. For the council, I think we can recommend the six-week Hina no-take rule, but only with a provisional boundary that’s jointly defined. And the landing monitoring should be designed to flag where boats actually go, not just whether they avoided Hina. I’ll hold off on a voucher amount until I see the ledger and can put the registered-only and, um, the broader dependent-recipient cases side by side.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mara Tui
transcript.text: I’d put one condition alongside that. The joint boundary work needs formal recognition of who monitors and what authority they have. Otherwise we may create disputes between patrol staff and rights holders right at the point of enforcement. I’ll check whether the people consulted so far can properly speak for the marriage- and residence-based users before we describe that process as representative.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: That sounds like the right condition. I’ll keep the ecological wording conditional too. It’s a May–June no-take area only once the jointly mapped landmark-and-route boundary covers the core counts and those suspect approach routes. Otherwise, we risk protecting the stations on paper and not the fish. I can put the route notes and the off-date lengths into a simple map for that boundary discussion.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes
transcript.text: That works for me. The map will also tell us whether landing-site records can plausibly distinguish a short shift to the north edge from a genuinely longer, costlier displacement. Right now, I don't think we know that. I'll wait for that and the voucher ledger before I turn the support scenarios into anything more definite.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Moana
transcript.text: Okay, I think we can give everyone a few minutes back. Thanks, both. I’ll circulate the map material once I’ve pulled it together, and then we can- we’ll pick this up next time.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Reyes

The dialogue supports some seed elements: patrol cannot enforce household quotas and rights holders would support bounded landing-site monitoring (turn 3); a six-week May-June Hina no-take approach is discussed (turns 3, 15, 20, 22); and support must account for pooled/dependent recipients rather than only registered boat owners (turns 10-14, 17-18). However, Leilani never states the required species-identification rationale or that any retention during aggregation undermines protection, Daniel does not affirm use of existing council fuel-voucher funds for lowest-income registered households rather than tradable quotas, and the group does not settle the recommendation. Instead, they leave the boundary, representation, displacement, voucher amount, and support eligibility unresolved and provisional (turns 19-23).

ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style, with mostly short-to-medium turns during setup and discussion but long, highly structured monologues during presentations. Participants frequently use backchannels (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), greetings, and light small talk before shifting into a more formal seminar register. There are occasional overlaps, false starts, repeated words, and self-corrections, especially in spontaneous questions and introductions; speakers often hedge with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “you know,” and “I guess.” Questions are usually prefaced warmly—“I have a quick question,” “this may be naive,” “great talk”—then develop into multipart, exploratory prompts. Challenges are indirect and collaborative rather than adversarial, often framed as extensions, uncertainties, or alternative possibilities. Presenters answer at length, acknowledge limits explicitly, and use cautious claims, while organizers keep transitions brisk with concise cues such as “okay,” “any more questions,” and “should we go to the next one.”

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.

Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
